The Transformer relies solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely [3]. Specifically, it eschews recurrence and relies entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output [2]. It is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution [1].

The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three ways: encoder-decoder attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder output), encoder self-attention (keys, values, and queries all from the previous encoder layer), and decoder self-attention (each position attends to positions up to and including itself, with masking to preserve the auto-regressive property) [4].

LoRA reduces trainable parameters by freezing the pretrained model weights and injecting trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture [1]. Specifically, for a pretrained weight matrix W₀ ∈ Rᵈˣᵏ, the update is constrained by a low-rank decomposition W₀ + ΔW = W₀ + BA, where B ∈ Rᵈˣʳ, A ∈ Rʳˣᵏ, and the rank r ≪ min(d, k) [4]. During training, W₀ is frozen and receives no gradient updates, while only A and B contain trainable parameters [4]. Because the rank r is small, the number of trainable parameters is greatly reduced [1][4]. Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times [1].

The models are trained on a weighted variational bound objective [2]. This simplified, weighted variational bound is derived from a novel connection established between diffusion probabilistic models and denoising score matching (with Langevin dynamics) [1][2]. The authors obtained their best sample quality results using the particular parameterization that reveals an equivalence with denoising score matching over multiple noise levels during training and annealed Langevin dynamics during sampling [3][4].

The two components combined in RAG are a parametric memory and a non-parametric memory [1][3].

The parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq transformer (BART), which serves as the generator: it conditions on the retrieved latent documents together with the input to generate the output [1]. The non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever (Dense Passage Retriever, DPR), which provides latent documents conditioned on the input [1].

These components are combined in a probabilistic model trained end-to-end, whereby both the generator and retriever are jointly learned [1].

DPO does not require a separate reward model because it uses a change of variables to define the preference loss as a function of the policy directly, rather than using the preference model to first train a reward model and then optimize a policy against it [1]. This works through a new parameterization of the reward model that enables extraction of the corresponding optimal policy in closed form, allowing the standard RLHF problem to be solved with only a simple classification loss [4]. In effect, DPO identifies a mapping between language model policies and reward functions, so training the language model to satisfy human preferences directly with a simple cross-entropy loss produces the optimal policy to an implicit reward function fit to the preference data—without explicit reward modeling [2][3].

The Transformer contains no recurrence and no convolution, so it must inject information about the relative or absolute position of tokens in the sequence [1]. To do this, it adds "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks [1]. These positional encodings have the same dimension dmodel as the embeddings, so the two can be summed [1]. In the base model, sine and cosine functions of different frequencies are used, with PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/100002i/dmodel) and PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos/100002i/dmodel), where pos is the position and i is the dimension; the wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π [1].

The authors also experimented with replacing the sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings, observing nearly identical results to the base model [3].

LoRA introduces no additional inference latency because its simple linear design allows the trainable matrices to be merged with the frozen weights when deployed [3]. Specifically, in production one can explicitly compute and store W = W0 + BA and perform inference as usual, since both W0 and BA are in R^{d×k} [1]. This construction guarantees that no additional latency is introduced during inference compared to a fine-tuned model [1]. When switching to another downstream task, W0 can be recovered by subtracting BA and then adding a different B′A′, a quick operation with little memory overhead [1].

A trained DDPM generates a new sample by running the reverse process, a parameterized Markov chain. It first draws xT from the prior p(xT), then iteratively samples each xt from the learned conditional pθ(xt|xt+1) for t = T−1, ..., 0, ultimately returning x0 [1][3]. The reverse process transitions are set to conditional Gaussians, made possible because the forward diffusion adds only small amounts of Gaussian noise [4].

In these experiments T = 1000, so sampling requires 1000 neural network evaluations, with the reverse process represented by a U-Net backbone (similar to an unmasked PixelCNN++) with self-attention at the 16×16 resolution [3]. The reverse process is trained directly as a latent variable model, with sampling interpretable as annealed Langevin dynamics under a particular parameterization [4].

The RAG-Sequence model uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete output sequence, treating the retrieved document as a single latent variable that is marginalized to obtain the seq2seq probability via a top-K approximation [2]. In contrast, the RAG-Token model can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly, which allows the generator to choose content from several documents when producing an answer [2].

This distinction is also described at a high level: one formulation conditions on the same retrieved passages across the whole generated sequence, while the other can use different passages per token [6].

They also differ at decoding time. RAG-Token behaves as a standard autoregressive seq2seq generator, so its per-token transition probability can be plugged into a standard beam decoder [3]. RAG-Sequence's likelihood does not break into a conventional per-token likelihood, so it requires running beam search per document and additional forward passes (using "Thorough" or "Fast" decoding) [3]. For sequence classification tasks (target class as a length-one sequence), the two models are equivalent [2].

DPO optimizes a policy using a simple binary cross entropy objective, producing the optimal policy to an implicit reward function fit to the preference data [1]. It solves the standard RLHF problem with only a simple classification loss [6]. The optimization objective is equivalent to a Bradley-Terry model with a reward parameterization r*(x,y) = β log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)), optimized as a single maximum likelihood objective, bypassing both fitting an explicit reward and performing RL [3].

BERT uses two unsupervised pre-training tasks [3]. The first is the "masked language model" (MLM), which randomly masks some tokens from the input, with the objective of predicting the original vocabulary id of the masked word based only on its context. This enables the representation to fuse both left and right context, allowing pretraining of a deep bidirectional Transformer [2]. The second is a "next sentence prediction" task, which jointly pretrains text-pair representations [2].

The Vision Transformer converts an image x ∈ R^(H×W×C) into a sequence of flattened 2D patches x_p ∈ R^(N×(P²·C)), where (P,P) is the patch resolution and N = HW/P² is the number of patches, which serves as the effective input sequence length [2]. Since the standard Transformer expects a 1D sequence of token embeddings, the flattened patches are mapped to D dimensions with a trainable linear projection, producing what the authors call the patch embeddings [2]. Similar to BERT's [class] token, a learnable embedding is prepended to the sequence, and its state at the encoder output serves as the image representation [2]. Standard learnable 1D position embeddings are added to the patch embeddings to retain positional information [2]. This resulting sequence of embedding vectors then serves as input to the Transformer encoder [2][3].
